about: Each session's default run of show, for a 75-minute session. Each entry in `weeks` is one session (week 0 is Prep), and the site seeds a new cohort's sessions from this file, and every scene stays editable in the class builder. Scenes use the site's shape (assets/show-lib.js on the site branch): kind, title, minutes, body (what the main stage shows), and config. Written by Claude from docs/research/curriculum/00-curriculum-design.md, October 7, 2026, awaiting Ben's review. A scene's optional `note` is for the teacher only, and a week's `questions` go into the cohort's question bank (kind, prompt, choices, points).

weeks.title: Cohort Prep: getting set up and meeting your group
weeks.question: What do I need in order to build at all?

scenes.title: Arrive
scenes.body: Your name, where you are joining from, and one thing in your life you wish worked differently. That last line is the first entry in the log you start tonight.

scenes.title: How we talk to one another
scenes.body: The four rules, said aloud: no correcting what does not matter, no acting surprised, no taking over, and no small digs at who someone is. When one is broken, someone says so plainly, the person says thanks, and we move on.

scenes.title: Show what you set up
scenes.body: In your group's room, each person opens their app's address on their phone and holds it up. If setup stopped somewhere, show where it stopped, and the group works through it together. Being stuck tonight is the most useful thing anyone can bring.

config.prompt: Show your app's address on your phone, or where setup stopped, and say one thing in your life you wish worked differently.

scenes.title: What a bring-back looks like

I did something the long way because nothing helped. Someone I know struggled with the same thing. No app ideas yet, just what happened. Write today's line now, before you leave: this log is where week 1's problem comes from.

weeks.title: Week 1: finding a problem worth building for
weeks.question: What problem in your own life is worth building something for, and who else has it?

scenes.title: Arrive
scenes.body: One line in the chat from your noticing log: the one you keep thinking about. Then what I read in your answers last session, and what I changed because of them.

scenes.title: Show what you brought back
scenes.body: In your group's room, each person reads from the log they kept for five days.

scenes.note: Watch for log lines that are already app ideas ("an app that..."), and steer back to what happened.

scenes.title: Computer-shaped and human-shaped
scenes.body: A computer-shaped problem is one a database and some code can take control of: counting, sorting, reminding. A human-shaped problem is something in your life that has gone unsolved for months or years, that you wonder about often, and that you cannot do yourself with the tools you have. It is about people's stories more than data points. This week you choose one, and your agent stays closed until you have, because the problem has to be yours before anyone helps.

scenes.title: Hold one to the tests
scenes.body: With your agent closed, take the log line you keep coming back to and write it as a problem: what happens in your life, then "I need something that..." Put it on the board and hold it to the ten tests in stage 00, marking each yes, not yet, or I don't know. A "not yet" is the next thing to find out, not a failure.
scenes.note: Watch for a problem that names a technology. Ask what happens in their life instead.

scenes.title: Start
scenes.body: Before you leave, name two people who might have this problem, and write three questions for them that each start "Tell me about the last time you..." Do not describe an app. This week is stage 00, then stage 01 once your problem holds: the smallest real version, live with real data, in the hands of one of those two people.

weeks.title: Week 2: the first app, and the same app on a second device
weeks.question: What has to be the same on every device, and what should feel as if it was born there?

scenes.title: Arrive

scenes.body: In your group's room. Each person in turn: say what you want to know, show it on the device, and explain one decision with your agent closed (a decision, never the code). scenes.title: Two layers
scenes.body: Every app built from the template has two layers. The data plane holds what is the same everywhere (what exists, what is allowed, and what it is called), and it is built once. The native layer holds what should feel born on each device: its controls, its gestures, and its look. Archive Watch's contract says it in one line: no client re-implements or re-hosts any part of the pipeline. Tonight you sort your own app into those two layers.

scenes.title: One verb, twice
scenes.body: Write the one thing your app must do on every device. Then draw it twice: once on the device you started with, and once on the device your people reach for next, each with that device's own controls. Mark what lives in the data and what lives in the device.

scenes.title: Start
scenes.body: Write the one rule about your data that every platform must follow. Then, before you leave, send the first prompt of stage 02: ask your agent to read your parity matrix with you and trim what your app does not need. Stage 03, a second platform that feels born there, follows once the matrix is honest.

weeks.title: Week 3: proof that it works, and someone else's hands
weeks.question: How do I know it works, and what happens when someone I did not build it with holds it?

scenes.title: Arrive
scenes.body: One line in the chat: the cell in your parity matrix that your own eyes proved wrong. Then what I read in your answers last week, and what I changed.

scenes.title: Show what you brought back
scenes.body: In your group's room. Each person in turn: say what you want to know, show it on the device, and explain one decision with your agent closed (a decision, never the code). The others ask one question to understand it, then answer the three questions: where is it going, how is it going, and what is next. The builder ends by saying what they will do next, and ready or not yet.

config.prompt: Show your matrix and the cell your eyes proved wrong, then your app on the oldest device it supports: the newest feature that device will not show, and why the new look fits your people.

Explain one decision, agent closed
One question, then the three answers
What is next, and ready or not yet

scenes.note: Watch for a second platform that only runs in a simulator, and for a look that is still the template's.

scenes.title: Why the agent cannot grade itself
scenes.body: An agent reports what it intended. "I fixed it" is true about the code and says nothing about the app, and everything short of the real device lies a little: the simulator allows what a real device forbids, and a log line that says "shown" does not mean a person could read it. So the agent does the testing, and the evidence comes from outside it: a picture of the actual screen, a number read from the device, or a person holding it. The agent is never the tester.

scenes.title: What would you ask to see?
scenes.body: Take one thing your agent said it fixed this week. On the board, write the prompt you would send asking it to prove the fix, and what the screen would look like if the fix had not worked. Then read a partner's, and change yours if theirs asks for better evidence.

scenes.title: Start

Then plan stage 05: the person who will hold your app this week, the device they will hold it on, and the free way it gets there, a link, a test track, or the web.

scenes.title: Numbers that tell the truth
scenes.body: Once other people hold your app, you can no longer see it by using it yourself, so you read numbers about it. Stage 06's rules keep those numbers honest. A reader that cannot read says so, and a missing number is empty, never zero. Count only what servers and stores already see, with no tracking added to the app. And a number you aim at stops telling you the truth, so you read it, you do not chase it.

scenes.title: From reason to rule to check
scenes.body: Values climb. A reason is the "Why we build" paragraph your agent weighs like advice. A rule is a standing instruction in your own words, dated the day the agent crossed a line. A check is a test that fails when the line is crossed, so the agent cannot cross it without being told. Stage 08 is where your app's lessons climb, so the next app starts knowing them.
